title: Indian-American Hanu Karlapalem Wins National STEM Endorsement in Alabama State House Race
excerpt: The Madison-based tech entrepreneur and NAACP leader is challenging a two-term Republican incumbent while fighting a proposed amendment that would bar naturalized citizens from holding office.
body:
• Hanu Karlapalem, a naturalized US citizen from India, received a national STEM endorsement for his Alabama State House District 4 campaign
  • The Madison resident of 26 years is challenging two-term Republican incumbent Parker Moore in the November 3 general election
  • Karlapalem is also fighting SB21, a proposed Alabama constitutional amendment that would ban naturalized citizens from holding state office
  • His platform focuses on lowering costs for families, strengthening public schools, and expanding healthcare access in North Alabama

A STEM Endorsement for a Tech Entrepreneur

Hanu Karlapalem, an Indian-American technology entrepreneur running for the Alabama State House of Representatives, has received a national STEM endorsement for his campaign in District 4 — a recognition of his background in technology and his advocacy for science and engineering education in North Alabama.

The endorsement adds to a growing list of credentials for Karlapalem, who is the Democratic nominee in the November 3, 2026, general election. He faces two-term Republican incumbent Parker Moore in a district covering portions of Morgan, Limestone, and Madison counties — a region at the heart of Alabama's aerospace and defense corridor.

From India to Alabama's Political Arena

Karlapalem moved to the United States from India and has been a Madison, Alabama resident for 26 years. He earned a Master of Science in Management Information Systems from the University of Alabama in Huntsville and founded Vinhamz Inc., a consulting firm specializing in network and cloud services. He brings more than three decades of experience in business, engineering, and information technology.

His civic involvement runs deep. He has served as Second Vice President of the Limestone County NAACP, sat on the UAH Alumni Association board, chaired the Asian American and Native Hawaiian Pacific Islander Caucus of the Alabama Democratic Party, and served on the State Democratic Executive Committee. He previously ran for Madison mayor in 2016 and for the Limestone County Commission in 2018.

Fighting a Ban on Naturalized Citizens

Karlapalem's campaign carries additional weight because of SB21, a proposed Alabama constitutional amendment pushed by the Republican supermajority that would bar naturalized US citizens from holding public office in the state. Karlapalem has called the measure a direct attack on the 14th Amendment.

"I swore an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States," Karlapalem said in a campaign statement. "My loyalty is to that Constitution — not to kings, not to special interests, and not to any party above the law."

Platform and Outlook

Karlapalem's campaign is built on three governing principles — Economy First, People First, and Constitution First. His core issues include lowering utility costs for Alabama families, strengthening public schools, and expanding healthcare access. He has pointed to his 26-year record of community service as evidence of his readiness to tackle the district's infrastructure and healthcare challenges.

District 4 has never had a serious Democratic challenger, making this race a potential bellwether for immigrant political participation in Southern US politics. For the Indian-American community, Karlapalem's candidacy represents a growing trend of Indian-origin Americans seeking elected office at the state level, particularly in technology-driven regions.
